Sure thing! Happy to help. At first, you will absolutely need cash. You can do a number of ways of getting into rentals. The most common is called "house hacking". You basically buy a house, live in it for a few years, then move out, and rent it out to someone, and move to the next place and repeat.

This is ok, but you will eventually run into the problem of only allowed to have 10 loans through FHA/Fannie/Freddie on your own personal name.

To raise cash in the beginning, some people cash out 401k's (that's what I did, paid a LOT in taxes though), borrow from a friend/family member, crowd fund, sell items they have, or simply sacrifice and save. While I did cash out my 401k, I did have to sacrifice for a while. That means no latest iphone, no eating out, buying a used car instead of new, etc.

It sucks. But you're not worried about that. You're focused on the future.

Basically, live by this one phrase: You're living a life now that most people don't want to, to live a life later that most people can't afford to.

Anyway, when you start off, just keep rolling your profits into another rental, and another rental. To give you an idea, I started this back in 2011, and I've made a total profit of around $200k, not including equity I've got built up across all my rentals. Including my rental equity, I'm closer to $500k. Now, it's VERY tempting to go out and buy shit for yourself because you've earned it.

DO NOT DO THIS.

To give you an idea, out of that $200k profit over 5 years, I've used about $300 on myself. I took my wife to see Up, and I took my cousin to see The Force Awakens.

Other than that, I've just saved the money until it reaches a certain point, then use that money towards the down payment of another rental.

So, how do you get past the 10 loan limit?

Commercial financing on single family homes.

It sucks. Believe me. BUT, there's a bunch of advantages. First off, you need 20-30% down. That's not negotiable. So, for a $100k property, you need $20k-$30k for the down payment, plus closing costs.

Secondly, get a property manager. Yes, they will take 10% of your gross rents, but they deal with quite literally everything. They get someone into the property, do evictions, collect rents, take care of repairs (you can tell them you want to do the repairs if you're so inclined), etc, etc. Trust me, they are worth it. At the end of the month, they will cut you a check after all the expenses and wire it to your account.

You will also need to set up an LLC. You'll want this to protect yourself in case you get sued. Talk to a CPA and a real estate attorney. It won't be too spendy, but be prepared to spend a couple of bucks on them. They WILL save you headaches down the road.

Back to commercial financing, once you've got a business relationship set up with a bank, you provide proof of funds (bank statement), and simply pick a house, and they work out the paperwork. To give you an idea, I recently called my banker (VP of commercial lending), and simply gave her an address and said I was going to buy it. She already has my property manager's contact information, and they worked out everything behind the scenes. The banker then next day aired the documents to my house (I invest in St. Louis, MO, but I live in Washington State), and I signed them and returned them to her. That Saturday, I went to my bank, did a wire transfer to the title company, and I owned the house a few days later. Fairly painless.

They don't care about debt to income ratios, 10 loan limits, or anything like that. They care that the property's rents will cover the mortgage, likely repairs, insurance, etc. As long as the property will do that, they will lend me money all day long (as long as I've got the down payment as well). Because of this set up, it's quite possible to make say $50k a year, but have $500k in commercial loans.

Now, onto the meat of your question. How do I do this with no cash at the point where I'm at?

Two ways:

First, roll the profits into the next down payment, OR, my more favorite way:

BRRRR method.

Buy Rehab Rent Refinance Repeat

My personal house has about $100k in equity. I can take out a Home Equity Line Of Credit, or HELOC. I'm going to keep the numbers basic, so I don't have to type all day long, but you'll get the gist. :)

So, this $100k is available to me however I see fit. I pay 1% per month in interest, so $100k used, would be $1,000 a month.

So, I find a house I like. It's pretty good, but a bit dated. It's listed for $80k

I have a quick formula I use, which is After Repair Value * 80%, - repairs = Offer.

So, let's say the property is listed at $80k, and after some needed upgrades will be worth $100k (very common).

So, I make an estimate of $10k for repairs (Maybe new A/C unit, paint, new cabinets, flooring, whatever)

So, I offer $70k. I tell them I've got cash, and I'll close in a week.

If you want to include closing costs in this, offer them say $65k, but to keep it simple, we'll go with $70k offering.

Anyway, some people will say yes, some will say no.

We'll go on the assumption they say yes. :)

So, you take your HELOC, and take out $80k (70k offered price, and 10k for repairs). You're paying $800 a month for this privilege once you do.

Then, you do the repairs that are most needed, and will provide the best chance of higher appreciation. (Your property manager will likely have a realtor on staff, so you can ask them if you're not sure)

So, you're all in for $80k

Then, you have the property manager get a tenant into your property (This has historically taken me about 3 months from start to finish).

Once you have a tenant paying say $1,100 a month, you go to the bank and go:

"I own this property outright, and I've got a tenant with a signed lease paying $1,100 a month. I want to do a cash out refinance".

They say ok, and send out an appraiser.

Assuming the appraisal comes back at $100k, they will cut you a check for $80k ($100k - 20% down payment).

Then, you take that $80k and pay off the HELOC.

Then you repeat the process.

Now, you'll have to adjust the numbers so you can get it down to where you don't have to pay any cash out of pocket once it's said and done, but you get the idea. Even under this scenario, you're paying around $5k for closing costs (once for the initial purchase, and once for the cash our refinance), and $2,400 for the monthly HELOC payments (3 months worth @ $800 a month).

So even if we didn't adjust the numbers, you're paying $7,400 total out of pocket when it's all said and done for a $100k house that has upgrades in it, that if you went the "normal" way of paying out 20% down, you'd be paying $20,000 for the down payment plus the $2,500 in closing costs.

So, it's $7,400 vs. $22,500. Savings of over $15,000, AND you are making WAY more money in terms of percentages of your investment.

Then, simply repeat the process, and adjust accordingly.

If you get lucky, and it's rare, you can adjust the numbers down to where you actually MAKE money buying a house. I wouldn't count on that, but just letting you know what's out there.
